options.text: Random Output Memory
Read-Only Memory
Rewritable Optical Memory
Rapid Operating Memory

explanation: ROM stands for Read-Only Memory. Data can be read from it but cannot normally be written to during regular operation. It is used to store firmware that the system needs at startup.

text: What is the key difference between ROM and RAM?

options.text: ROM is faster than RAM
ROM is non-volatile — retains data without power; RAM is volatile and loses data when powered off
ROM can be written to freely; RAM cannot
ROM is used for temporary storage; RAM is used for permanent storage

explanation: The critical difference is volatility. ROM is non-volatile — its contents survive when the power is switched off. RAM (DRAM/SRAM) is volatile — all data is lost the moment power is removed. This is why the BIOS is stored on ROM, not RAM.

text: What is ROM typically used to store in a computer?

options.text: The user's documents and files
The operating system while it is running
Firmware such as the BIOS/UEFI — the startup instructions
Temporary data that the CPU is currently processing

explanation: ROM stores firmware — the low-level instructions the computer needs before the OS loads. The BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) or UEFI is stored on a ROM chip on the motherboard. It runs hardware checks (POST) and locates the OS at startup.

text: What does PROM stand for, and what makes it different from standard ROM?

options.text: Programmable ROM — can be written to once by the user, then becomes permanent
Protected ROM — has a hardware write-protect switch
Portable ROM — can be removed and used in other systems
Parallel ROM — reads multiple bits simultaneously for speed

explanation: PROM (Programmable ROM) comes blank from the factory and can be programmed once by the user using a special PROM programmer device. Once written, the data is permanent and cannot be changed or erased — unlike EPROM or EEPROM.

text: How is data erased from an EPROM?

options.text: By applying a high voltage electrical pulse
By exposing it to ultraviolet (UV) light through a quartz window
By running a software erase command from the OS
By removing power for an extended period

explanation: EPROM (Erasable Programmable ROM) has a small quartz window on the chip. Exposing it to UV light for around 15-20 minutes erases all stored data, after which it can be reprogrammed. The window is usually covered with a sticker to prevent accidental erasure from sunlight.

text: What makes EEPROM more practical than EPROM for modern use?

options.text: EEPROM is faster to read than EPROM
EEPROM can be erased and rewritten electrically without removing it from the circuit
EEPROM does not require power to retain data
EEPROM has higher storage capacity than EPROM

explanation: EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable ROM) can be erased and reprogrammed using electrical signals while still installed in the circuit — no UV lamp, no chip removal needed. This is why modern BIOS/UEFI chips use EEPROM, allowing firmware updates to be applied in software.

text: Which two statements correctly describe non-volatile memory? (Choose two)

options.text: Data is retained when power is removed
Data is lost when the computer is switched off
ROM is an example of non-volatile memory
DRAM is an example of non-volatile memory

explanation: Non-volatile memory retains its data without power — ROM, SSDs, and hard drives are all non-volatile. DRAM is volatile (data lost on power off). Non-volatile is essential for anything that needs to survive a reboot, like firmware and stored files.

text: Match each ROM type to its correct description.

columnB.text: Factory programmed, cannot be changed at all
Blank from factory, programmed once by user — then permanent
Erasable using UV light through a quartz window, then reprogrammable
Erased and rewritten electrically — used for modern BIOS/UEFI chips

explanation: The ROM family goes from least to most flexible: ROM (fixed forever) → PROM (written once) → EPROM (UV erasable) → EEPROM (electrically erasable). Each generation solved a limitation of the previous one. Modern BIOS chips are EEPROM, allowing firmware updates without replacing the chip.

text: A technician updates the BIOS firmware using a software utility downloaded from the manufacturer. Which type of memory is the BIOS chip most likely?

options.text: DRAM
PROM
EPROM
EEPROM

explanation: Because the update is done in software without removing the chip or using UV light, it must be EEPROM — which can be erased and rewritten electrically while still installed. PROM can only be written once, and EPROM requires UV light erasure.

text: Which of the following correctly summarises the volatile vs non-volatile distinction?

options.text: Volatile = keeps data without power; Non-volatile = loses data without power
Volatile = loses data without power; Non-volatile = keeps data without power
Both types lose data without power but at different rates
Volatile memory is always faster; non-volatile is always slower

explanation: Volatile memory (DRAM, SRAM) loses all data the moment power is cut. Non-volatile memory (ROM, SSD, HDD) retains data indefinitely without power. This is a fundamental distinction and a very common exam question.
